World War Two. Fought from 1939 to 1945 between the Axis Powers—Germany, Italy, Japan—and the Allied Powers including Britain, the Soviet Union, the United States, and numerous others, killing an estimated 70 to 85 million people and reshaping global politics, technology, and morality. It was the deadliest and most destructive war in human history, encompassing genocide, total warfare, nuclear weapons, and the emergence of two superpowers that would dominate the Cold War era.

Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party exploited Germany's postwar resentment and economic collapse, using the Treaty of Versailles to justify territorial expansion and the pursuit of Lebensraum—living space—for the Aryan race. Germany's invasion of Poland on September 1st, 1939, triggered Britain and France to declare war. Germany's subsequent blitzkrieg conquered France, the Netherlands, Belgium, and threatened Britain in the Battle of Britain from 1940 to 1941.

Japan's militarism in Asia led to the invasion of Manchuria in 1931, China in 1937, and eventually French Indochina. Italy under Benito Mussolini expanded in Ethiopia and the Mediterranean. The three Axis powers coordinated but rarely achieved perfect synchronization.

Germany's surprise invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, known as Operation Barbarossa, opened a titanic two-front struggle. The Eastern Front became the war's bloodiest theater, with the Siege of Stalingrad from 1942 to 1943 and the Battle of Kursk in 1943 among history's deadliest battles. The Allies invaded Normandy on D-Day, June 6th, 1944, establishing the Western Front and beginning the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi occupation.

The Holocaust—Nazi Germany's systematic genocide of six million Jews, along with millions of Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners, and others—represents history's deadliest act of mass murder and the nadir of industrial-scale atrocity.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7th, 1941, brought the United States into the war. The subsequent island-hopping campaign by the U.S. moved steadily toward Japan's homeland. Germany surrendered unconditionally on May 8th, 1945 after Hitler's suicide. Japan fought until the U.S. dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima on August 6th and Nagasaki on August 9th, 1945, killing hundreds of thousands and prompting Japan's surrender on September 2nd.

The war cost approximately 70 to 85 million lives. The Soviet Union alone lost over 27 million. Civilian deaths exceeded military deaths, and entire cities and industries were reduced to rubble.

The Yalta Conference in February 1945 and the Potsdam Conference in July 1945 divided postwar Europe into Allied occupation zones, partitioning Germany and establishing Soviet hegemony over Eastern Europe—the seeds of the Cold War. The United Nations was founded in April 1945 to prevent future global wars. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted in 1948 in response to the Holocaust.

Germany and Japan were demilitarized and rebuilt under U.S. and Soviet influence. The world emerged bipolar, with the U.S. and Soviet Union as superpowers, initiating a nuclear-armed standoff that would define the next 45 years.

World War Two crystallized the horrors of total war and industrial genocide, shattered the Eurocentric world order, and thrust nuclear weapons into human hands. The war spawned existentialism as a response to meaninglessness. It traumatized a generation and gave rise to psychoanalytic critiques of fascism and authoritarianism. The Holocaust remains the paradigm case of systematic dehumanization. The war's technology—radar, jets, rockets, nuclear fission—rocketed humanity into the atomic age. Its territorial redrawing, including the division of Korea, the partition of India, and the birth of Israel, set the stage for late-twentieth-century conflicts. The war's moral accounting—Nuremberg trials, war crimes definitions, human rights law—fundamentally changed how civilization reckons with atrocity.
